title: The Rise of China

cards.h: A fishing town became a megacity in one generation
cards.b:
In 1980, Shenzhen near Hong Kong was a small market town of a few tens of thousands. Today it holds over 17 million people and makes much of the world's electronics.

Shenzhen is the symbol of China's economic rise.

After Mao, Deng Xiaoping let farmers sell surplus crops, opened special economic zones and welcomed foreign investment. He is credited with the phrase about not caring if a cat is black or white if it catches mice (a saying he used).

With cheap labour and big ports, China exported huge quantities. After joining the WTO in 2001, growth soared, averaging near 10 percent a year for decades. China became the world's second-largest economy in 2010.

The World Bank says about 800 million people in China left extreme poverty since 1978.

China combined one-party rule with market growth. The 'one-child policy' (1980-2015) cut births but left an ageing population. China's population began to shrink in 2022.

Under Xi Jinping (leader since 2012-13), China launched the Belt and Road Initiative (2013), strengthened party control, and built a stronger navy.

Disputes arose over the South China Sea, Taiwan, trade and technology, and Hong Kong's 2020 National Security Law. The US sees China as its main rival. China argues it is reclaiming its place after the 'century of humiliation'.

As of 2025, China remains the world's second-largest economy, but faces slowing growth and a property slump.

cards.h: Is China's rise inevitable or fragile?
cards.b:
Some see unstoppable growth. Others point to debt, an ageing population and limited political freedom. Remember: China was the world's biggest economy for much of history before the 1800s, so many see this as a return.

Caution: 'poverty reduction' numbers depend on the poverty line used.

Neighbours, rivals, partners

China is India's neighbour, rival and partner. After the 1962 war, ties froze for years. In the 2000s trade grew fast. By 2023–24 China was India's largest trading partner, at about 118 billion dollars.

Yet the border stayed tense. On 15 June 2020, in the Galwan valley in Ladakh, 20 Indian soldiers died in a clash. India banned many Chinese apps and tightened rules on investment. Modi and Xi met at Wuhan in 2018, and in October 2024 the two sides agreed on border patrolling arrangements.

Both are in BRICS and both are rising, so the rivalry and the partnership continue side by side. Figures are as of 2024.

Five things to remember

  1. Reform began in 1978.
  2. Shenzhen and the WTO powered exports.
  3. China became No. 2 in 2010.
  4. Xi's China launched Belt and Road in 2013.
  5. India-China ties remain tense but linked.

Think about it

  • Is rapid growth possible without political freedom?
  • How should India deal with a powerful neighbour?
